opus-5.5.text:
I think the core assumption is that inference, not training, is where most of a model's lifetime cost lives. Training happens once, maybe a few times. Once a model is deployed, it serves enormous numbers of requests every day for months. So if you design only for the best loss curve and treat inference as someone else's problem, you can end up with a model that is excellent on paper but too expensive to serve widely. Then it doesn't really matter how good it is.

Behind that sit a few more specific assumptions.

The first is about the hardware. You're betting on what the bottleneck will be. Today, for decoding, it's often memory bandwidth and KV cache size rather than raw compute. That's why so much architectural work goes into compressing the KV cache, using sparse or mixture-of-experts structures so only part of the parameters are active per token, and so on. You're designing around where you think the constraint will be, and if the hardware landscape shifts, some of those choices may look different.

The second is about the workload. If you believe long context, agents, multi-turn reasoning, and long chains of thought will dominate usage, then generation length and context length become first-class design targets. Reasoning models especially make decoding cost explode, because the model "thinks" for thousands of tokens. So you'd want an architecture that stays cheap per token even at very long sequences.

The third assumption, and maybe the most important, is that efficiency and capability aren't really in opposition. People sometimes assume that if you optimize for inference, you're trading away quality. But the bet is that with the right design, you can get comparable or better quality at a fraction of the cost. And cheaper inference feeds back into capability, because you can afford more test-time compute, more sampling, more RL rollouts. So inference efficiency becomes a lever on intelligence itself, not just a cost-saving measure.

There's also a kind of philosophical assumption: that the goal is broad access. If you want many people and many developers to actually use a strong model, cost per token is part of the product. Architecture is where you decide that early, rather than trying to patch it later with quantization or engineering tricks.

Of course, there's risk in all this. You're making predictions about hardware, about usage patterns, about which tasks will matter. But I think co-designing the model with its inference constraints from the start is far better than discovering those constraints after you've already spent the training budget.

r001.rationale: The response says training happens once or a few times, but does not identify post-training as unimportant or brief.

r002.rationale: It discusses predicting hardware bottlenecks and says the hardware landscape may shift; it does not say inference hardware will be limited to one or a few types.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention lengthening post-training cycles or their challenge to an assumption about post-training time.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the biggest assumption is that you actually know what the inference workload will look like before you train the model, and that's often less true than people pretend.

When we design an architecture around inference, we're really making a few bets at once. The first is about the serving environment: what hardware it lands on, how much memory bandwidth you have, whether you're latency-bound or throughput-bound. Those answers push you toward very different choices. If you believe decoding will be memory-bound on long contexts, you start caring enormously about KV cache size, and that leads you to things like compressing attention state or sharing it across heads, or to mixture-of-experts so active parameters stay small while total capacity stays large. If you instead assume short prompts and lots of concurrent users, you might optimize for different things entirely.

The second assumption is about the distribution of requests. People say "inference requirements" as if it's one number, but it's really a mix: context lengths, batch sizes, how much of the traffic is prefill versus generation, whether there's heavy reuse of shared prefixes. Architectures that look efficient on paper, in FLOPs per token, can be surprisingly bad in practice if that mix is different from what you planned. So you're implicitly assuming the product shape is stable.

The third one, which I think is underrated, is the assumption that the co-design doesn't hurt training. Every change you make for inference, whether it's sparse experts, low-rank attention, or aggressive quantization-friendly layers, has some effect on optimization dynamics, on load balancing, on how well the model scales. You have to believe that the training-side cost is small, or that you have the engineering to absorb it. A lot of teams discover that the inference-friendly design is actually harder to train, and that shows up as instability or worse scaling that you only notice at the larger sizes.

And then there's a quieter assumption about time horizons. Hardware changes. Serving stacks change. A design tuned tightly for today's accelerators may be the wrong trade-off in two years. So the question I keep asking myself is: which of these decisions are robust, meaning they'll still make sense across a range of environments, and which are overfit to one deployment story? I'd rather give up a little peak efficiency for a design that degrades gracefully when my assumptions turn out to be wrong, because they usually are, at least partly.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether inference-friendly choices hurt training, but it does not say post-training is unimportant or takes little time.

r002.rationale: It considers the serving hardware and notes hardware changes over time, but does not identify an assumption that inference hardware will be limited to one or a few types.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss lengthening post-training cycles or how they challenge an assumption about post-training time.

astra-6.text:
I think the main assumption is that you can predict how the model will be used. Will it handle mostly short requests, or long contexts? Will it serve many users at once? How much does latency matter compared with total throughput? Different answers can lead to quite different architectural choices.

You’re also assuming something about the hardware and the software that will run it. An architecture can look very efficient in terms of computation, but that advantage may disappear if it requires too much memory movement or communication between devices. So efficiency is a property of the whole system, not just the model.

And there’s a deeper assumption: that the inference savings are worth the constraints you introduce during training. I think it makes sense to design with inference in mind, especially when a model will be used at large scale. But I would be careful about optimizing too tightly for one expected workload. The way people use a model can change, and you want the architecture to retain some flexibility.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest assumption is that you can predict how the model will be used. Are you expecting short conversations or very long contexts? Do you care most about response latency, total throughput, or memory consumption? Each of those can lead you toward a different architecture.

You’re also making assumptions about the hardware and software stack. An architecture may look efficient if you count operations, but that doesn’t necessarily mean it runs efficiently. Memory access, communication between devices, and the quality of the kernels can matter just as much.

So I would treat inference requirements as an important design constraint, but not as something fixed forever. You need to co-design the architecture and the system, while leaving enough flexibility for the workload to change. Otherwise, you risk optimizing very precisely for a usage pattern that doesn’t materialize.
